proposals.name: Tonal Control Across Shifts
proposals.instruction: Score high if the story maintains a coherent emotional/tonal register throughout, and if the tone does shift, the shift is deliberately staged and reinforced (e.g., via refrain, escalation, or framing) so it reads as a controlled effect. Score low if the story lurches between incompatible tones -- e.g., whimsical or cute imagery collides with grim or violent content, or a serious emotional beat is undercut by a jokey aside -- in a way that reads as accidental or unresolved rather than intentional.
proposals.rationale: R13 sustains a single elegiac register (the refrain 'To serve is the highest honour') through both the mundane opening and the death scene, and R16 never breaks its ironic essayistic voice even in its digressions. By contrast R19 swings unreconciled from cutesy nursery-room description to a sudden, unironic confessional prayer about serial murder, and R22 undercuts its own torture-scene tension with a jokey 'see you in your nightmares, kiddies' author's note.

proposals.name: Stakes Earned Through Accumulated Detail
proposals.instruction: Score high if emotional or dramatic stakes are built up through concrete scene-work, physical detail, or accumulating incident, so the reader arrives at the feeling rather than being told to have it. Score low if a major emotional event (death, danger, loss) is simply announced or asserted with little scene-work behind it, so the stated magnitude of the event and the felt weight of the prose don't match.
proposals.rationale: R30 builds its stakes through repeated concrete physical struggle ('gripped the traces,' 'sat hard, my whole weight crushing her into the sand') layered onto the stated fact of 'sixteen generations,' and R13 earns its grief through sensory build rather than assertion. By contrast R31 announces 'the rents are dead' mid-gossip with zero scene development, and R20 never builds any stakes at all around its one-line premise.

proposals.name: Self-Conflicted or Ambiguous Motivation
proposals.instruction: Score high if a character's motives are shown to be mixed, self-deceiving, or genuinely conflicted, and the story lets that ambiguity stand rather than resolving it into a simple label. Score low if characters act from a single, stated, uncomplicated motive with no interior friction, especially when a character exists mainly to move the plot or deliver a line.
proposals.rationale: R09's narrator explicitly interrogates their own possibly-selfish motives for 'good deeds' ('I'm not selfless -- I'm someone who recognized that doing a good thing for someone else felt good... felt power over them') without resolving the ambiguity, and R18 gives Mason genuine suppressed resentment toward the friend he depends on. By contrast R02's bureaucrat-aliens and R33's angel/demon duo act from single flat motives (efficiency, banter) with no interior complication.

proposals.name: Structure That Enacts Its Own Theme
proposals.instruction: Score high if the story's form (repetition, recursion, fragmentation, framing device) is doing thematic work -- the shape of the telling mirrors or embodies what the story is about, not just decorates it. Score low if the story is told in a default, generic scene-then-scene order with no relationship between structure and content, even if that structure is competently executed.
proposals.rationale: R28's stuttering, miscounted '1, 2, 3... 24. Sorry. 24. Or was it 72?' prose rhythm formally enacts the temporal disorientation the time-loop story is about, and R06's recursive premise (a story about itself, revised as its own revision-count updates) makes its form and content the same object. By contrast R01 and R03 are told as straightforward, competently sequenced scenes with no structural relationship to their content.

proposals.name: Implied World Beyond the Frame
proposals.instruction: Score high if the story conveys history, institutions, or culture through specific, unexplained detail dropped in passing (names, numbers, rituals, titles) that implies a larger world without stopping to explain it. Score low if world-facts are delivered as direct exposition -- a character explains the setting's mechanics to another character or the reader mainly to convey information.
proposals.rationale: R30's 'Sixteen generations' and unexplained ritual call 'Eyyyoh,' and R40's footnoted in-world historical document citing specific races, dates, and prior wars, both gesture at vast unseen history through implication. By contrast R14's villain explains his own vault's specs aloud ('ninety-eight TZ-1200 super computers...') purely to inform the reader, and R02's aliens narrate Earth's political history to each other as as-you-know-Bob dialogue.

proposals.name: Sensory and Imagistic Specificity of Prose
proposals.instruction: Score high if the prose uses unusual, precise, or vivid sensory images (sight, smell, texture, sound) that could only belong to this particular scene. Score low if description is generic, minimal, or interchangeable with countless other stories -- the scene is conveyed almost entirely through dialogue or plot beats with little independent sensory grounding.
proposals.rationale: R05 sustains an extended, strange, cosmic sensory register ('tearing at the delicate edges of our own spacetime as she tickled her fancies, wet her lips on succulent new places to haunt') and R27 renders numbness through precise small sensations ('the sun hurts my eyes, even through the sunglasses'). By contrast R08 and R26 convey their scenes almost entirely through back-and-forth dialogue with minimal independent sensory description.

proposals.name: Ending Deepens Rather Than Resolves
proposals.instruction: Score high if the final beat retroactively adds a new layer of meaning to what came before, so the story is more resonant after the ending than before it. Score low if the ending is a 'gotcha' or punchline that merely resolves curiosity or lands a joke without adding thematic weight -- remove it and the rest of the story loses little.
proposals.rationale: R37's ending (humanity stripped of speech as punishment) recontextualizes the entire courtroom-plea scene as a story about the danger of language itself, and R09's closing line ('I'm done comparing') reframes the narrator's self-justification as self-aware moral failure. By contrast R25's '5:01. Quitting time.' and R14's tab-count punchline resolve their jokes cleanly but add no further meaning to what precedes them.

proposals.name: Extreme Content in Service of Theme
proposals.instruction: Score high if disturbing, violent, or crude material functions to reveal character psychology or advance a coherent theme, such that the difficulty is doing narrative work. Score low if extreme content appears primarily for shock or titillation, disconnected from character development or a thematic throughline, especially if the story itself winks at or undercuts its own seriousness.
proposals.rationale: R04's serial-killer narrator remains psychologically coherent throughout -- every killing is filtered through her stated logic of protecting her friend -- and R15's body-horror escalates in service of a specific arc about denial and transformation. By contrast R22's torture scene builds tension only to cap it with a flippant 'see you in your nightmares, kiddies' note, and R19's grim backstory is delivered as an unearned devotional monologue disconnected from any characterization built earlier.

proposals.name: Distinctiveness of Narrative Voice
proposals.instruction: Score high if the prose has a specific, idiosyncratic verbal fingerprint (diction, syntax, rhythm) that would let a reader identify this narration among many others. Score low if the narration reads as generic or interchangeable -- competent, unremarkable sentences that could belong to any story in the genre.
proposals.rationale: R16's baroque, digression-loving essayistic voice ('the true ceremony hidden behind the paper of the contract... eating the decorative swan at a banquet') and R40's dry in-world historian's register are both unmistakably specific. By contrast R01 and R11 are told in competent but generic narration with no particular verbal signature.

proposals.name: Narration Carries Atmosphere Beyond Dialogue
proposals.instruction: Score high if the story builds mood, interiority, or physical stakes through narrated prose, not only through what characters say to each other. Score low if the story is carried almost entirely by dialogue exchange with minimal independent narration doing descriptive or psychological work.
proposals.rationale: R05 and R27 both sustain long stretches of interior, atmospheric narration independent of dialogue. By contrast R02, R08, R20, R23, R25, and R33 are constructed almost entirely as back-and-forth banter, with narration reduced to brief tags between lines of dialogue.

proposals.name: Premise Explored as Sincere Inquiry
proposals.instruction: Score high if the story treats its central conceit as something worth genuinely examining, following its implications into new or uncomfortable territory. Score low if the conceit exists solely to set up a single joke or reveal, after which the story has nothing further to say about it.
proposals.rationale: R27 follows its 'numbing virus' premise into real existential territory (declining birthrates, the erosion of what makes people feel human) rather than stopping at the initial irony, and R09's 'afterlife leveling' premise is used to interrogate the narrator's own moral self-image. By contrast R20's 'god on a budget' story exists to deliver one platypus joke, and R23's whale-military parody exists to sustain a single pun conceit without further development.

proposals.name: Interpretive Work Left to the Reader
proposals.instruction: Score high if the story conveys its central meaning, backstory, or emotional truth through implication -- juxtaposed images, gaps, or indirect cues -- trusting the reader to assemble it. Score low if the story states its meaning, backstory, or moral outright, especially through a character explaining their own feelings or history in direct expository terms.
proposals.rationale: R21 conveys its entire dream/coma logic through unexplained visual cues (a parent's body blurring into another, faces that look 'split') with no narrator explanation, and R28's disorientation is conveyed through broken counting rather than description of confusion. By contrast R19 has its 'misunderstood villain' backstory explained directly and completely through an on-the-nose prayer monologue that states outright what the story is supposedly discovering.

proposals.name: Commitment to a Non-Human Value System
proposals.instruction: Score high if a non-human narrator's priorities, vocabulary, and moral logic are genuinely different from a human's -- not just human characters relabeled with animal or alien nouns. Score low if a nominally non-human narrator thinks, values, and speaks exactly like a contemporary human in costume (same institutions, slang, and priorities, just with a species label swapped in).
proposals.rationale: R13's dog-guard narrator operates from an entirely alien value hierarchy (service as the 'highest honour,' a cosmology of the 'Field After,' an internal ritual called 'One-of-Nine') with no human equivalent. By contrast R23's whales run a human navy complete with sergeants, radio jargon, and gossip about 'that dolphin girl,' and R33's angels and demons trade contemporary slang ('dickwads') indistinguishable from human action-movie banter.

proposals.name: Escalation Without Repetition
proposals.instruction: Score high if each successive scene or beat adds new information, raises the stakes, or changes the situation, so the story keeps developing until its end. Score low if the story reaches its point early and then repeats variations on the same beat (the same joke, the same exchange, the same tension) without further development before ending.
proposals.rationale: R30 escalates continuously from the egg cracking to the physical struggle to the final vow, each beat changing the situation. By contrast R25's call-center dialogue cycles through several near-identical troubleshooting exchanges that restate the same joke rather than developing it, and R11's list of chained mishaps, while amusing, is a flat recitation rather than an escalating scene.

proposals.name: Pacing That Lets Tension Build Before the Turn
proposals.instruction: Score high if the story allows sufficient narrative space and rising pressure before its climax or resolution, so the turn feels earned by what preceded it. Score low if the climax and resolution are compressed into a small fraction of the story's length relative to its setup, so the ending feels rushed or arrives before the reader has been given time to feel the stakes.
proposals.rationale: R07 spends extended space building dread about the extortion gang before the confrontation, letting the father's calm resolve land with weight, and R18 lingers in psychological setup before its plot mechanics kick in. By contrast R01 compresses an entire discovery-confrontation-banishment arc into a single page with almost no build between the sister's warning and the demon's defeat, and R11's entire chain of chaos is delivered in one breathless retrospective paragraph rather than experienced scene by scene.

proposals.name: Sustained in-world idiolect in the narration
proposals.instruction: Judge whether the narrating voice thinks in the concepts its own world would supply, rather than neutral contemporary author-English draped over a costume. Clearly satisfying: the narrator names things as its culture or species would and the reader must translate ('the Great-Long-Lived', 'the Field After', 'We-The-Small'; an alien officer's log that calls whiskey a 'noxious potion' and humans 'skin-beasts'; an in-universe containment manual with its own dating convention and clinical euphemisms). Clearly failing: narration could be lifted into any other story unchanged, and a demon, a whale, or a gargoyle-keeper perceives and phrases things in default modern idiom, with genre proper nouns supplying all the flavor. Do not credit invented names alone; credit invented frames of reference. Score 1 = fully generic narration, 5 = a self-consistent conceptual vocabulary sustained to the last line.
proposals.rationale: R03 and R29 sit at dense_pct .966/.972 with card_pct .146/.154 and are almost pure idiolect performances: R03 never once uses the words 'dog' or 'human', R29 is written as an alien survival manual. R08 (dense .937, card .096) is only two paragraphs long, so a scorecard has little structure to reward, yet the entire piece is a committed alien register. Against these, R16 (dense .082, card .927) and R26 (dense .122, card .898) have vivid casts but narrate them in interchangeable modern prose. A bank scoring 'strong voice' generically will not separate these; a bank scoring conceptual translation will.

proposals.name: Premise delivered by inference, not restated as exposition
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the writing prompt's setup the story hands back to the reader as explanation versus dramatizes and lets the reader assemble. Clearly satisfying: the prompt's central conceit is never named in the text at all, or is named only once and late, and the reader infers it from behavior, diction, and detail (a physics-classroom dialogue in which the narrator's ability to see through walls is never mentioned and is legible only in which question he asks; a guard's devotional monologue from which the reader must deduce the species of both parties). Clearly failing: the opening paragraph paraphrases the prompt as narration or as a character's speech, then the rest illustrates the paraphrase; or a character states the premise aloud to another character who already knows it. Judge only the delivery, not whether the premise is interesting. Score 1 = premise restated then illustrated, 5 = premise fully load-bearing yet never stated.
proposals.rationale: R21 (dense .921, card .098) hides the entire prompt inside the shape of a student's question and never claims the power; R03 (dense .966, card .146) never names what its narrator is. The opposite pole is where the scorecard is highest: R09 (dense .158, card .971) opens by stating the budget conceit and then explains the platypus, and R19 (dense .182, card .993) is a three-line statement of its own premise. R16 (dense .082, card .927) literally recites 'alien ghost zombies' from the prompt in dialogue. Restatement reads as 'answers the prompt' to a criterion bank and as inertness to a reader.

proposals.name: Affect held flatter than the events warrant
proposals.instruction: Score the gap between the magnitude of what is being reported and the temperature at which the narrator reports it, and whether that gap is controlled rather than accidental. Clearly satisfying: massacre, extinction, genocide, or self-horror is narrated in an even, domestic, or bored register, and the flatness is itself characterizing ('And the blood. So much blood... He sighed. Whatever.'; a species-wide sterilization reported as 'How... interesting.'; interbreeding-or-elimination of every peer civilization filed as a statistics lesson; a serial killer describing stakings in the cadence of friendship gossip). Clearly failing: the prose supplies the emotional label for the reader at every beat ('rage ensnared her in its thorny coils'), or a horror set-piece is scored with adjectives telling the reader it is horrifying. Also failing: flat narration of low-stakes material, which is merely flat. Score 1 = affect fully pre-chewed for the reader, 5 = a wide, deliberate, sustained disproportion.
proposals.rationale: This is the single most consistent feature of the dense-high half: R04 (dense .986, card .097) narrates human extinction at a shrug; R14 (dense .846, card .013) reports the elimination of every near-peer species as an aside; R39 (dense .939, card .095) and R34 (dense .986, card .139) both let monstrousness pass unremarked by their narrators. The dense-low, card-high half labels its emotions: R31 (dense .179, card .964) and R16 (dense .082, card .927) tell the reader what to feel at each turn. A bank crediting 'emotional impact' or 'vivid emotional language' will invert this exact contrast.

proposals.name: Narrator understands less than the reader does
proposals.instruction: Judge whether the story is built so the reader sees past the narrator, and whether that gap is sustained rather than closed by an explanatory line. Clearly satisfying: the narrator sincerely reports what he sees, and the reader assembles a second, truer story out of the same sentences (a devoted guard interpreting a human deathbed through the theology of service; a woman inside a fabricated world reporting that her parents' bodies look 'split' and then going back to sleep; a narrator recounting his species' behavior with pride while the reader reads it as an indictment). Clearly failing: the narrator glosses his own situation, tells the reader what the irony is, or the story stops to explain its own device. A neutral case is a fully knowing narrator with no gap at all; score that in the middle only if nothing is lost by it. Score 1 = story explains itself, 5 = a sustained gap that the reader must close and that the ending does not close for them.
proposals.rationale: R03 (dense .966, card .146) and R33 (dense .918, card .060) both depend entirely on a narrator who cannot name her own predicament; R14 (dense .846, card .013) is unreadable as anything but unintentional self-indictment. The card-favored rows do the reverse: R28 (dense .170, card .960) narrates its own construction and revision count, and R19 (dense .182, card .993) explains its joke in its final sentence. Explicit self-explanation reads as 'clarity' to a criterion bank.

proposals.name: Central pressure is interior and not solved by the plot
proposals.instruction: Identify what is actually at stake and whether the story's events dispose of it. Clearly satisfying: the real problem is the narrator's standing, dependence, shame, obligation, appetite, or self-understanding, and the external events leave it exactly where they found it or make it worse (a support-class party member who survives every fight and still ends the scene salvaging crystals alone while the others laugh; an initiate who wins the hatching and is left with the fear the hatching was supposed to cure; a man who has enumerated his own charity and concluded he is not good). Clearly failing: the stated problem is an external obstacle, the story removes it, and nothing inside anyone has changed (the hex is diagnosed and escalated to a specialist; the demon is sprayed and flees; the curse is cured and they walk home). Score 1 = the story is entirely an obstacle removed, 5 = an interior pressure that the events sharpen rather than resolve.
proposals.rationale: R01 (dense .969, card .072) and R25 (dense .947, card .126) both end with the protagonist's private problem intact and heavier; R24 (dense .935, card .110) has no plot at all, only a self-assessment. The mirror image scores high on the card: R36 (dense .129, card .972) and R30 (dense .020, card .932) are clean problem-introduced/problem-eliminated shapes, and R07 (dense .071, card .880) resolves entirely in the principal's office. A bank with criteria for 'clear conflict' and 'satisfying resolution' will systematically prefer the second group.

proposals.name: Form enacts the condition it describes
proposals.instruction: Judge whether sentence length, syntax, repetition, line-breaking, or layout do work that the content also does, so that the reading experience reproduces the state on the page. Clearly satisfying: lethargy written in short flat clauses that trail into ellipses and refuse to build; a time loop written as counting, restarts, and self-correcting fragments; incomprehensibility written in self-cancelling syntax ('holding her close to me, or far away from me, or all of it, at once'); a refrain that returns as ritual rather than as reminder. Clearly failing: a distinctive psychological or metaphysical condition delivered in undifferentiated well-made paragraphs that would serve any other subject equally; or formal oddity with no relation to content (decorative line breaks, arbitrary dividers). Score 1 = form indifferent to content, 5 = form and content inseparable.
proposals.rationale: R04 (dense .986, card .097) and R12 (dense .945, card .095) would both be judged 'choppy' and 'underdeveloped' by any conventional prose criterion, yet their choppiness is the content; R02 (dense .998, card .139) is the strongest case in the slice, its grammar performing the incomprehensibility it claims. Meanwhile R31 (dense .179, card .964) and R36 (dense .129, card .972) deliver captivity-horror and workplace-magic in identically smooth paragraphing. This criterion is where a mechanics-and-structure bank most reliably penalizes the thing a reader most rewards.

proposals.name: Ending leaves live pressure rather than sealing the story
proposals.instruction: Judge the final movement. Clearly satisfying: the last lines land on an unresolved obligation, a decision not yet paid for, or a consequence the reader can feel arriving, and the story trusts that to be enough ('Sixteen generations. Gods damn it, I would have to fly.'; a truce with one's own trapped life reached over eggs and bacon; the bandits still walking up the road). Clearly failing: the last lines tie the situation off with a mutual agreement, a restored status quo, a shared drink, or an explicit signal that the adventure is over ('Pub.' / 'ready to commit more misadventures' / the appointment is booked and the shift ends). A story may end quietly and still score high; the test is whether anything is still owed. Score 1 = fully sealed and consequence-free, 5 = closed as a scene but open as a life.
proposals.rationale: R01 (dense .969, card .072), R25 (dense .947, card .126), and R38 (dense .886, card .036) all stop with the weight still on the character. The card-high rows close hard: R05 (dense .067, card .935) ends on a companionable 'Pub.', R06 (dense .071 range, card .905) ends on 'ready to commit more misadventures', R26 (dense .122, card .898) ends with the favour accepted. 'Has a clear resolution' is one of the most standard rubric lines in existence, and here it points the wrong way.

proposals.name: Value survives deletion of the final line
proposals.instruction: Mentally delete the last sentence or paragraph and ask what remains. Clearly satisfying: the piece still has a voice, a situation, and a felt interior after the ending is removed; the ending deepens material that was already working. Clearly failing: removing the last line leaves an inert setup, because the whole text was a delivery mechanism for one reversal or gag (a three-line story whose only content is 'that's an autobiography'; a dialogue that exists to reach 'a duck with a beaver tail'; a chain of classroom mishaps that exists to reach 'Nelson's my boa'; an alien-accountant conversation that exists to reach a hairstyle joke). Note that a story can have a strong final turn and still pass, if the preceding text carries independent weight. Score 1 = pure punchline vehicle, 5 = value distributed throughout, ending as intensifier not as payload.
proposals.rationale: The card-high half is disproportionately punchline-shaped: R19 (dense .182, card .993), R09 (dense .158, card .971), R07 (dense .071, card .880), and R27 (dense .170, card .907) all collapse to nothing without their last beat, and all four are near the top of the scorecard. R11 (dense .924, card .035) and R24 (dense .935, card .110) survive amputation entirely. A bank crediting 'memorable ending', 'twist', or 'payoff' cannot distinguish a payoff from a payload.

proposals.name: Detail is selected under pressure, not inventoried
proposals.instruction: Judge whether concrete details are chosen because this character, in this moment, would register them, or listed because description was called for. Clearly satisfying: detail arrives through action and fear and does characterizing work (feeding an arm through a harness and shaking it loose, gripping traces, the hot sand, the membrane the hatchling shreds; blood on a companion's teeth noticed exactly when he is being friendly). Clearly failing: an unbroken inventory of furnishings, brands, and colors that any narrator would produce identically (carpet, dresser, laptop, entertainment center, television, posters, in list order), or spec-sheet accumulation used as a substitute for scene. High density of nouns is not the test; motivated selection is. Score 1 = catalogue, 5 = every detail load-bearing for the person perceiving it.
proposals.rationale: R25 (dense .947, card .126) and R01 (dense .969, card .072) both filter their worlds through a body under stress. R35 (dense .131, card .976) spends its opening on a room inventory and R32 (dense .179, card .964) on invented hardware specifications; both sit near the scorecard ceiling. Any criterion of the form 'uses vivid, specific sensory detail' counts nouns and therefore rewards the catalogue.

proposals.name: Specifics invented rather than drawn from the genre shelf
proposals.instruction: Score the proportion of the story's named material that the author made versus borrowed. Clearly satisfying: the world's texture comes from invention at the level of the sentence, and the inventions imply a history ('the War of Too Many Uncles', the age of poisoned perfumes, a peasant poet replaced at his own wedding by a trained ferret; a rule of 'first exposure-first extinction' with a named victim system and a named observing species). Clearly failing: the story runs on off-the-shelf furniture supplied by the genre or the prompt itself, with flaming swords, tridents, archangels, pit lords, dwarves, and cursed steeds doing the work that invention should do. Borrowed figures are allowed if the story does something to them; the failure is borrowing as substitute. Score 1 = entirely stock, 5 = a specific invented history implied on nearly every page.
proposals.rationale: R11 (dense .924, card .035) is almost nothing but invention and is the second-lowest scorecard row in the slice; R29 (dense .972, card .154) invents a whole diplomatic history. R16 (dense .082, card .927) and R06 (dense .067 range, card .905) are assembled from stock pieces and score near the scorecard top. A bank crediting 'worldbuilding' by counting proper nouns treats Beelzebub and 'the House of Many Mirrors' as equivalent.

proposals.name: Figuration earns its reach; no decorative simile drag
proposals.instruction: Evaluate the figurative language specifically. Clearly satisfying: comparisons extend the story's own physics or psychology and could not be swapped out (a god who takes an incomprehensible beloved to a supernova because it is the only burning he understands; light from an extinguished source still arriving and preventing sleep). Clearly failing: similes that are locally clever but drag in an alien register or a joke the story cannot afford, breaking the point of view (whale sonar laughter compared to 'ripples seen after a fat man tries the cannonball in a kiddie pool'; a bottle of bleach christened a 'peacemaker' mid-terror; a dry voice 'like sandpaper against a tree'), or figuration applied uniformly as decoration regardless of tension. Score 1 = decorative or POV-breaking figuration, 5 = every figure native to the story's own logic.
proposals.rationale: R23 (dense .062, card .862) and R30 (dense .020, card .932) are the two clearest cases of well-formed similes that leak register or pre-digest emotion, and both are near the scorecard ceiling; R31 (dense .179, card .964) is the same pattern. R02 (dense .998, card .139) is the counterexample: its figures are the story. A criterion bank almost certainly rewards 'uses figurative language effectively' by presence, which is exactly the wrong direction here.

proposals.name: Tension sustained rather than defused by reflexive quipping
proposals.instruction: Judge whether characters are permitted to be inside their situation, or whether every beat is immediately neutralized by banter. Clearly satisfying: dialogue and narration let discomfort, dread, or humiliation stand; humor, when present, comes from the situation rather than from characters performing wit at each other. Clearly failing: mortal or uncanny stakes punctuated by trade-off one-liners so that no beat is allowed to land ('Hell ain't frozen over yet, dickwads' delivered mid-slaughter; a curse-breaking scene played entirely as rump-slapping and lunch jokes; a resurrection scene that never stops trading insults). Note that a story can be wholly comic and still score high if the comedy is the pressure rather than an escape from it. Score 1 = every beat defused on arrival, 5 = the story holds its own discomfort.
proposals.rationale: R16 (dense .082, card .927), R06 (card .905), and R05 (dense .067, card .935) all run on continuous banter and all sit above the scorecard's 90th percentile. R34 (dense .986, card .139) and R01 (dense .969, card .072) refuse the relief valve entirely. Quip density looks like 'natural, engaging dialogue' and like 'voice' to a rubric, so this is a likely site of over-crediting.

proposals.name: A speaking presence, judged separately from clean mechanics
proposals.instruction: Ask whether some particular person is audibly behind the sentences, and score that independently of spelling, grammar, and formatting. Clearly satisfying: an unmistakable individual pressure in the prose even where the surface is rough, with typos, run-ons, or lowercase drift that do not erase the speaker. Clearly failing: fluent, error-free, well-organized prose behind which no one is present, because it is procedural, template, or boilerplate text that could have been produced by an institution rather than a person. Judge presence, not correctness; a piece with perfect mechanics and no speaker should score at the bottom, and a misspelled piece with a live voice should not be penalized here (penalize mechanics elsewhere if the bank wants them). Score 1 = no one home, 5 = an unmistakable individual voice.
proposals.rationale: R18 is the diagnostic row: an automated subreddit removal notice, mechanically flawless and perfectly structured, at dense_pct .007 and card_pct .805. Whatever the bank is scoring, that row passes it. R33 (dense .918, card .060), R39 (dense .939, card .095), R17 (dense .921, card .098), and R14 (dense .846, card .013) all have visible surface errors and sit near the dense ceiling and the card floor. The bank appears to be reading correctness as quality and to have no criterion that fires on 'nobody wrote this'.

proposals.name: Abstraction anchored to an unexpected concrete particular
proposals.instruction: For any story working in abstraction, lyric, or interior generality, judge whether it lands on specific matter and whether the particular chosen is surprising rather than stock. Clearly satisfying: a meditation on lost control of time that resolves into eggs, bacon, toast, 'eh, some lettuce, for health', and a hope about tomorrow's bacon; cosmic abstraction pinned to Saturn's rings, a supernova, and the frozen instant before crushing at a black hole's center. Clearly failing: sustained abstraction whose only concretes are the genre's default emotional furniture (starlight, horizons, dreams, hearts) so that nothing in the piece could belong to one person and no one else. Score 1 = free-floating sentiment with interchangeable images, 5 = abstraction repeatedly earthed on particulars that only this speaker would choose.
proposals.rationale: R12 (dense .945, card .095) and R02 (dense .998, card .139) are both abstract pieces that keep touching specific matter. R40 (dense .062, card .845) is a competent lyric whose images never leave the prompt's own supplied vocabulary of stars and light, and it sits at the scorecard's upper band; R19 (dense .182, card .993) is generality with no particular at all. A bank scoring 'imagery' or 'poetic language' by presence cannot see the difference between an image and a default.

proposals.name: Protagonist implicated without exculpation offered
proposals.instruction: Judge whether the story arranges sympathy for its central figure or lets the reader see them at cost. Clearly satisfying: the narrator supplies the evidence against himself and declines to argue it away ('I don't think I truly did anything for someone else... felt power over them. Someone told me I changed their life immeasurably - I was fucking hooked'; a killer whose account of her own motives never quite reaches her own actions; a man whose revulsion at what he did turns, unremarked, into appetite). Clearly failing: the story pre-loads justification so that the protagonist is safe before the reader can judge (the wronged party is unambiguously monstrous, the violence is unambiguously defensive, the sympathetic reading is stated by another character, or a villain's cruelty is redescribed as a sacred duty the text endorses). Score 1 = fully exculpated and morally safe, 5 = implicated, with the reader left holding the judgment.
proposals.rationale: R24 (dense .935, card .110), R39 (dense .939, card .095), R34 (dense .986, card .139), and R01 (dense .969, card .072) all decline to protect their narrators, and all four are dense-high with card scores under .14. The card-high half is morally safe: R30 (dense .020, card .932) gives its protagonist an indisputable monster to destroy, and R35 (dense .131, card .976) resolves a serial murderer into a devout servant of God. 'Sympathetic, well-motivated protagonist' and 'character growth' are standard rubric lines and both reward the safe version.

proposals.name: Premise Transformation
proposals.instruction: Score high when the prompt’s premise drives a consequential change, discovery, or decision; score low when the story merely restates the premise or appends an unrelated gag.
proposals.rationale: R01 turns universal infection into emotional and reproductive extinction, while R06 makes the dragon’s difference a personal disability and inherited burden.

proposals.name: Psychological Contradiction
proposals.instruction: Score high when a character’s feelings, beliefs, and behavior meaningfully conflict; score low when reactions are emotionally obvious, uniform, or unsupported.
proposals.rationale: R18 pairs moral numbness with jealousy and dependence, and R22 admits altruism is motivated by self-importance rather than presenting virtue simply.

proposals.name: Reframing Reveal
proposals.instruction: Score high when later information substantially changes the meaning of earlier details; score low when the ending only confirms an obvious twist or supplies a disconnected surprise.
proposals.rationale: R19’s infection reverses the apparent human-versus-alien encounter, and R27’s coma revelation makes the seemingly ordinary world increasingly sinister.

proposals.name: Prompt-Specific Originality
proposals.instruction: Score high when the story finds a distinctive implication or angle that is tightly rooted in the prompt; score low when it follows a familiar genre template with interchangeable details.
proposals.rationale: R02 notices a philosophical consequence of measurement inside the cat experiment, while R31 recasts humans through the devoted dog’s ideological worldview.

proposals.name: Subtextual Density
proposals.instruction: Score high when concrete actions or dialogue communicate important unstated motives, relationships, or meanings; score low when every implication is explained directly.
proposals.rationale: R03’s breakfast decision quietly expresses an attempt to reclaim agency, and R31’s reverent language reveals dependence and grief without naming the humans as owners.

proposals.name: Earned Escalation
proposals.instruction: Score high when complications intensify through believable cause and effect and force changed stakes; score low when events simply pile up without altering the characters’ situation.
proposals.rationale: R06 escalates from hatchling danger to the protagonist’s concealed physical fear, and R40 moves from a child’s nightmare to a protective sibling relationship.

proposals.name: Narrative Economy
proposals.instruction: Score high when each paragraph, image, or exchange advances character, conflict, atmosphere, or meaning; score low when the piece is padded with exposition, repetition, or ornamental setup.
proposals.rationale: R36 achieves a complete comic situation in a few controlled paragraphs, whereas R17 spends extensive space on invented technical quantities before reaching its central joke.

proposals.name: Concrete Sensory Grounding
proposals.instruction: Score high when specific sensory details make the imagined situation physically immediate and reveal character or danger; score low when description remains generic, abstract, or merely decorative.
proposals.rationale: R06 uses wet shell, sand, harnesses, and bodily struggle to ground the dragon scene, while R40 makes the demon tangible through smell, fingerprints, teeth, and bleach.

proposals.name: Voice-Premise Alignment
proposals.instruction: Score high when diction, syntax, and figurative language consistently embody the narrator’s identity and the story’s premise; score low when the voice could belong to almost any narrator or shifts unintentionally.
proposals.rationale: R28’s unstable cosmic language embodies a reality-warping lover, and R31’s ritualistic pack vocabulary sustains the dog narrator’s worldview.

proposals.name: Tonal Control
proposals.instruction: Score high when shifts between humor, horror, tenderness, or absurdity are deliberate and mutually reinforcing; score low when tonal changes feel accidental or neutralize the intended stakes.
proposals.rationale: R21 makes overwhelming superpower violence coexist with petty legal trouble, and R40 balances grotesque horror with genuine sibling tenderness.

proposals.name: Character Agency
proposals.instruction: Score high when a protagonist makes a consequential choice based on a recognizable desire, fear, or value; score low when the character mainly observes events or is carried from setup to punchline.
proposals.rationale: R03 chooses a mundane ritual to resist temporal helplessness, and R38 shows the father deliberately deciding how to confront the extortion gang.

proposals.name: Social Consequence Worldbuilding
proposals.instruction: Score high when speculative rules produce believable institutions, customs, incentives, or social behavior; score low when worldbuilding is only a list of fantastical nouns.
proposals.rationale: R26 develops an economic marriage system whose incentives shape nobles and commoners, while R30 shows galactic strategy changing because of humanity’s broadcasting behavior.

proposals.name: Relational Specificity
proposals.instruction: Score high when a relationship is revealed through distinctive reciprocal behavior, history, or language; score low when characters function only as generic roles such as friend, victim, rival, or love interest.
proposals.rationale: R31’s dog and human communicate through caregiving rituals and shared mortality, while R40 establishes the sisters’ history through irritation, protection, and inherited coping knowledge.

proposals.name: Motif Payoff
proposals.instruction: Score high when a repeated word, image, ritual, or object accumulates meaning and returns with a changed emotional force; score low when repetition is filler or an isolated flourish.
proposals.rationale: R03 repeats counting and breakfast to track the narrator’s struggle with time, and R31’s repeated service maxim changes from doctrine into an act of mourning.

proposals.name: Substantive Completion
proposals.instruction: Score high when the ending leaves the reader with a developed emotional, ethical, or conceptual consequence beyond the initial premise; score low when the piece is only a setup, exposition dump, or single punchline.
proposals.rationale: R22 ends by exposing the vanity beneath both grandmother’s and narrator’s goodness, while R33 explicitly remains an account of writing with little story development.

proposals.name: Premise as story engine
proposals.instruction: Score high when the prompt’s unusual premise drives specific conflicts, choices, and consequences through the whole story; score low when it is merely mentioned or illustrated once.
proposals.rationale: R05 and R22 turn their premises into governing social situations, while R06 and R40 largely deliver a single literal joke about the prompt.

proposals.name: Distinctive narrative voice
proposals.instruction: Score high when diction, rhythm, attitude, and viewpoint create a recognizable narrator; score low when the prose could belong to almost any story.
proposals.rationale: R05 and R21 have unusually strong, sustained voices, whereas R13 and R27 rely more heavily on interchangeable exposition and banter.

proposals.name: Concrete sensory specificity
proposals.instruction: Score high when physical sensations, objects, spaces, and actions make the scene vivid and particular; score low when settings and reactions remain generic or abstract.
proposals.rationale: R11 and R15 use precise bodily and environmental details, unlike the largely generalized presentation in R06 and R27.

proposals.name: Self-implicating character complexity
proposals.instruction: Score high when a character’s motives contain meaningful contradiction, denial, or moral self-exposure revealed through behavior; score low when characters simply state or enact one uncomplicated trait.
proposals.rationale: R15, R29, and R35 complicate their narrators’ self-understanding, while R06 and R09 offer little interior conflict beyond the immediate gag.

proposals.name: Causal escalation
proposals.instruction: Score high when each development follows from earlier choices or revelations and intensifies the central problem; score low when events are merely piled on or summarized without causal pressure.
proposals.rationale: R11 and R34 build increasingly consequential turns from established actions, while R26 and R40 mainly stack genre elements or explanations.

proposals.name: Recontextualizing ending
proposals.instruction: Score high when the final beat changes how earlier material is understood while feeling prepared in retrospect; score low when it only repeats the premise or supplies an arbitrary punchline.
proposals.rationale: R07, R15, and R34 gain force from endings that reinterpret the preceding story, unlike the flatter closures of R06 and R40.

proposals.name: Form serving content
proposals.instruction: Score high when the chosen form—poem, transcript, document, dialogue, or other structure—actively conveys character, information, or theme; score low when formatting is ornamental or replaceable.
proposals.rationale: R10, R12, and R22 make poetic, dialogic, or documentary form part of the storytelling, whereas R31’s recursive format adds comparatively little beyond its concept.

proposals.name: Implied worldbuilding
proposals.instruction: Score high when social rules, institutions, history, or technology are revealed through consequences and specific practices; score low when the world is explained directly without being dramatized.
proposals.rationale: R21, R22, and R38 imply functioning cultures through customs and duties, while R04 and R27 frequently explain their worlds in abstract blocks.

proposals.name: Controlled tonal modulation
proposals.instruction: Score high when shifts among humor, horror, tenderness, or seriousness are deliberate and preserve the story’s underlying coherence; score low when tonal changes feel accidental or merely sensational.
proposals.rationale: R14, R19, and R34 coordinate absurdity with darker stakes, while R26 and R40 more often present escalation as disconnected spectacle.

proposals.name: Non-obvious interpretive angle
proposals.instruction: Score high when the story finds a fresh social, moral, or emotional implication in the prompt rather than using its most predictable reading; score low when it follows the prompt’s default joke or genre path.
proposals.rationale: R21, R29, and R38 derive unexpected implications from familiar setups, while R16 and R40 remain close to straightforward anthropomorphic or explanatory treatments.

proposals.name: Information density
proposals.instruction: Score high when nearly every sentence advances plot, character, atmosphere, or meaning without requiring extensive explanation; score low when the story spends many words restating context or delaying movement.
proposals.rationale: R05 and R10 achieve substantial effect in very little space, whereas R04 and R13 devote much of their length to background exposition.

proposals.name: Embodied nonhuman perspective
proposals.instruction: Score high when a nonhuman or altered narrator’s perceptions, values, metaphors, and assumptions remain consistently shaped by that condition; score low when the narrator is essentially a human voice wearing a costume.
proposals.rationale: R37 and R38 make cosmic and canine consciousness shape the narration, while R16 and R40 mostly give nonhuman entities ordinary human dialogue and reasoning.

proposals.name: Emotional afterimage
proposals.instruction: Score high when an image, choice, or final realization creates feeling that persists beyond the immediate plot or joke; score low when the piece ends without emotional residue once its premise is understood.
proposals.rationale: R29, R35, and R38 leave morally or emotionally unresolved impressions, unlike the quickly exhausted effects of R06 and R40.

proposals.name: Structural use of self-awareness
proposals.instruction: Score high when metafictional or self-aware narration changes the character’s situation, the reader’s interpretation, or the story’s causal structure; score low when fourth-wall awareness is merely a decorative aside.
proposals.rationale: R14, R23, and R36 use altered awareness to shape events and interpretation, while R31 largely comments on its own construction without developing consequences.

proposals.name: Controlled linguistic risk
proposals.instruction: Score high when unusual syntax, repetition, metaphor, or diction creates a deliberate effect while remaining intelligible; score low when experimentation becomes confusing, accidental, or indistinguishable from proofreading errors.
proposals.rationale: R10, R23, and R37 take substantial stylistic risks that remain coherent, whereas R39 and R40 contain roughness that more often obscures than enriches the intended effect.
